summary: A burrowing land turtle whose long tunnels shelter hundreds of other animals.
description: A large, dark brown to grayish-black land turtle with a shell 6 to 15 inches long.  Its hind feet are stumpy, like an elephant's, and its front feet are flattened like shovels for digging.  The lower shell is yellowish and has no hinge.
habitat: Open pine woods on sandy, well-drained soil, kept open by fire.
life: It digs burrows that are often more than 30 feet long.  About 60 kinds of vertebrates and 300 kinds of invertebrates take shelter in them.  A tortoise can live 50 to 80 years.
alabama: Only the tortoises west of the Mobile and Tombigbee Rivers are on the federal list, and in Alabama that is the southwest corner of the state.  East of those rivers the tortoise is not federally listed.
countiesText: Listed only west of the Mobile and Tombigbee Rivers
range: The coastal plain from South Carolina to eastern Louisiana, and peninsular Florida
threats: Loss, breaking up, and decline of its habitat, much of it from the loss of fire and of open pine woods.

summary: A large, glossy, blue-black snake of the sandhills that winters in gopher tortoise burrows.
description: A large, thick-bodied snake, glossy blue-black all over, with a chin and throat that may be reddish, orange-brown, or cream.  The young are black with narrow whitish-blue bands.  It is not venomous.
habitat: Longleaf pine sandhills, scrub, pine flatwoods, hardwood hammocks, and coastal dunes.  It shelters in the burrows of gopher tortoises.
life: It breeds from October through January, and the adults roam over large home ranges.  It lives 8 to 12 years in the wild.
alabama: Once a snake of Alabama's coastal plain.  The Encyclopedia of Alabama reports that it has been released in Conecuh National Forest to bring it back to the state, and that no established breeding population was known when that article was written.
countiesText: Conecuh National Forest; once the coastal plain
range: Parts of Florida, southern Georgia, and southern Alabama
threats: Loss and breaking up of habitat by building and roads, vehicle strikes, killing by people, and a rising sea.

summary: A large black constrictor of the longleaf pine country of southwest Alabama.
description: A snake that is black or dark brown above and below.  Some have a russet snout, white scales on the neck, or faint blotches toward the tail.  It is not venomous, and kills its prey by constriction.
alabama: Found in Clarke, Mobile, and Washington Counties.
threats: Loss of longleaf forest, snake fungal disease, vehicle strikes, and deliberate killing.  The populations that remain are small and cut off from one another, and inbreeding has begun to harm their health.

photoElsewhere.label: A photo by Kevin Narum, The Nature Conservancy, on the FWS site

summary: A small turtle with a flattened shell, found only in the upper Black Warrior River system.
description: A small aquatic turtle with a distinctly flattened shell, up to 4.7 inches long.  The shell is dark brown to orange, and the underside pink to yellowish.  It has two barbels on the chin and webbed feet.
habitat: Free-flowing creeks and small rivers, with shallows and with deeper pools swept by the current, where rocks and crevices give shelter.
life: It eats snails, mussels, clams, and water insects.  The adults are active mostly at night, from April to October.  Females do not breed until they are six to eight years old.
alabama: Found only in Alabama, in the Black Warrior River system upstream of Bankhead Dam.  It now holds an estimated quarter to a third of its former range.
threats: Silt is the greatest threat.  Dams, development, and collecting for the pet trade have also cut its numbers.

summary: A large plant-eating turtle of the Mobile-Tensaw Delta.
description: A large freshwater turtle with a shell 8 to 10 inches long, tall and arched, brown to olive with light upright bars.  The belly is usually orange to reddish.  The upper jaw has a notch at its tip with a tooth-like point on each side.
habitat: Shallow, weedy backwaters and river channels.  It depends on underwater plants for food, shelter, and places to bask.
life: It feeds almost wholly on water plants.
alabama: It lives around Mobile Bay and in the Mobile-Tensaw Delta, mostly in Baldwin and Mobile Counties.  Its main nesting ground in the state is Gravine Island, a degraded dredge-spoil site in the delta.  The Alabama population appears stable, but is not growing.
range: Alabama, and a small part of coastal Mississippi
threats: Dredging, pollution, development, bulkheads that block the way to nesting ground, predators at the nests, boat strikes, shooting, and deaths on roads.

seasonNote: Nesting season on Alabama beaches runs from May 1 through October 31
summary: The sea turtle Alabama sees most, and the only one that nests here every year.
description: A large sea turtle.  Adults average about 36 inches in shell length and 250 pounds.  The shell is reddish-brown to brown, and the underside yellow to brown.
habitat: The open Gulf and coastal waters.  The females come ashore on sandy beaches to nest.
life: A female lays about 80 to 120 eggs in a nest, and they hatch after about two months.
alabama: Loggerheads nest from the Florida line to Dauphin Island, most of them between Fort Morgan and Gulf Shores.
range: The Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans; Alabama's turtles belong to the Northwest Atlantic population
threats: On Alabama's beaches the chief danger is light.  Bright lights confuse nesting females and draw hatchlings away from the water, where they die of exhaustion, drying, or predators.  Shield or turn off lights that can be seen from the beach, and never use a white flashlight near a nest.
notes: The date above is that of the rule that listed the Northwest Atlantic population on its own.  The species was on the federal list before that.

seasonNote: Nesting season on Alabama beaches runs from May 1 through October 31
summary: A large sea turtle with a smooth, heart-shaped shell, and one of three kinds that nest on Alabama's beaches.
description: Adults can reach about 4 feet and 440 pounds.  The shell is heart-shaped and smooth, brown with dark blotches, and the underside is pale.  The head is small, and each flipper has a single claw.  Hatchlings are black above and white below.
habitat: Coastal Gulf waters.  The females nest on sandy beaches.
alabama: One of the three sea turtles that nest on Alabama's Gulf beaches, though far less often than the loggerhead.
range: Warm seas around the world; Alabama's turtles belong to the North Atlantic population
threats: On Alabama's beaches the chief danger is light, which confuses nesting females and draws hatchlings away from the water.
notes: The date above is that of the rule that listed the North Atlantic population on its own.  The species was on the federal list before that.

seasonNote: Nesting season on Alabama beaches runs from May 1 through October 31
summary: The smallest sea turtle, a crab-eater of shallow Gulf waters that sometimes nests in Alabama.
description: The smallest of the sea turtles, about 2 feet long and 100 pounds.  The adult has a nearly round, olive-gray shell and a triangular head with a hooked beak.  Hatchlings are black above and below.
habitat: Shallow coastal waters, where it feeds along the bottom.
alabama: One of the three sea turtles that nest on Alabama's Gulf beaches, though far less often than the loggerhead.
range: The Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic coast of North America
threats: On Alabama's beaches the chief danger is light, which confuses nesting females and draws hatchlings away from the water.  The five-year review covers the wider threats.

summary: The largest of all turtles, a deep diver of the open sea that passes through the Gulf off Alabama.
description: The largest sea turtle, usually 4 to 8 feet long and 500 to 2,000 pounds.  It has no hard shell.  Its back is a mosaic of small bones under tough, rubbery skin, with seven raised ridges running its length.  It is mostly black with pale flecks, and its paddle-like limbs have no claws.
life: It dives deeper and travels farther than any other sea turtle.
alabama: Leatherbacks are found offshore, in the Gulf waters off Alabama.  The state does not count it among the turtles that nest on its beaches.
threats: The profile read for this entry does not list threats.

summary: A reef turtle with a hawk-like beak, hunted for its shell, and a rare stray in Alabama's waters.
description: A small to medium sea turtle, 2.5 to 3 feet long, with a long oval shell whose plates overlap like shingles, a beak like a hawk's, and two claws on each flipper.  The shell is brown, splashed with yellow, orange, or red.
habitat: Rocky places, coral reefs, shallow coastal waters, and lagoons, seldom deeper than 65 feet.  It nests on quiet tropical beaches.
alabama: The Service's Alabama office counts the hawksbill among the sea turtles it answers for.  It is a turtle of tropical reefs, and the state's guide to its sea turtles does not mention it.
range: The Caribbean and the western Atlantic, among other tropical seas
threats: Hunting for tortoiseshell, which goes on through illegal trade, along with coastal development, lights on nesting beaches, pollution, boat strikes, and capture in fishing gear.

summary: The largest freshwater turtle in North America, proposed for listing as threatened.
description: A very large turtle with massive jaws and a rough, ridged shell that recalls the hide of an alligator.  Males can reach 249 pounds.  The females are much smaller.
alabama: The Service's Alabama office counts it among the species it answers for.  The sources read for this entry do not name the rivers.
countiesText: Not named in the sources read
range: Fourteen states of the Southeast, the Midwest, and the Southwest
threats: Harvest for meat, which emptied many rivers of large turtles, along with collecting, predators at the nests, drowning in fishing gear, swallowed hooks, and changes to its rivers.
notes: The Service proposed listing it as threatened in November 2021.  It has no row on the federal list as of the date this site was checked.

summary: No longer in danger, and kept on the federal list only because its hide looks like those of crocodilians that are.
description: The sources read for this entry do not describe the alligator, and few Alabamians need it described.
habitat: The sources read for this entry do not describe its habitat.
alabama: The Encyclopedia of Alabama notes that the alligator is neither threatened nor endangered in the state.  It stays on the federal list under a special rule, 50 CFR 17.42(a).
countiesText: Not named in the sources read
threats: None that put it on the list today.
notes: First listed in 1967, when it was in real danger.

summary: A river turtle named for the fine, map-like lines on its shell, listed because it is hard to tell from a rarer cousin.
description: A medium-sized turtle.  The females are 5.5 to 11.5 inches long and the males 3.5 to 5.  The brown shell bears faint orange, yellow, and green markings that look like the lines of a map.
habitat: Rivers and streams with sandy or muddy bottoms and with places to bask.
alabama: It lives in the Alabama, Tombigbee, Tensaw, Black Warrior, and Coosa Rivers and the streams that feed them.
range: The Mobile River system, in Alabama, Georgia, Mississippi, and Tennessee
threats: It is not judged to be in danger itself.  It was listed because it is so hard to tell from the Pearl River map turtle of Mississippi and Louisiana, which collectors take illegally.  Collecting it is now banned.

summary: A large map turtle of the rivers of south Alabama, listed because it is hard to tell from a rarer cousin.
description: A large river turtle.  The females reach about 11 inches and the males about 5.  The shell is olive green to tan, with light yellow markings shaped like circles or the letter C, which fade in old females.
habitat: Rivers only, and most of all where there are logs and sandbars.
alabama: Recorded in the Conecuh, Yellow, Pea, and Choctawhatchee Rivers.
range: The Escambia, Yellow, and Choctawhatchee river systems, in Alabama and Florida
threats: It is not judged to be in danger itself.  It was listed because it is so hard to tell from the Pearl River map turtle of Mississippi and Louisiana, which collectors take illegally.  Collecting it is now banned.

refs.label: FWS: questions and answers on the map turtle listings

summary: A big-headed map turtle of the rivers of southeast Alabama, listed because it is hard to tell from a rarer cousin.
description: A large river turtle.  The females are 8 to 12 inches long, with massive heads, and the males seldom pass 5 inches.  The shell is olive to tan, with light yellow markings shaped like circles or the letter C.
habitat: Rivers only, and most of all stretches with exposed limestone and with snags to bask on.
alabama: It lives in the large rivers of the southeast, chiefly the Chattahoochee and Choctawhatchee systems.
range: River systems of Alabama, Florida, and Georgia
threats: It is not judged to be in danger itself.  It was listed because it is so hard to tell from the Pearl River map turtle of Mississippi and Louisiana, which collectors take illegally.  Collecting it is now banned.

summary: A small, stout snake with an upturned snout, proposed for listing as threatened, and not recorded in Alabama since 1975.
description: A short, stout snake, usually 14 to 21 inches long, with a sharply upturned, pointed snout.  It is yellowish gray or light brown, tinged with orange-red on the back, with large, dark, squarish blotches down the spine and smaller ones on the sides.  The belly is cream.  It is not venomous.
habitat: Dry uplands of the coastal plain and sandhills: old fields, openings in the woods, and hardwood hammocks.
life: It is secretive, and spends much of its time under litter or underground.  It eats mostly toads, which it digs out with its snout.  When threatened it hisses, flattens its neck, and plays dead.  It does not bite.
alabama: It was once found in the Ridge and Valley country of central Alabama and in parts of the coastal plain.  The state knows of no record since 1975.  It may be gone from Alabama, or it may hang on in very low numbers.
range: The coastal plain of the Southeast.  The state names Georgia, South Carolina, and Florida as places where it still lives.
threats: It is declining throughout its range, and the state's account says the reasons are not known.
notes: The Service proposed listing it as threatened on August 29, 2025, and reopened the proposal for comment on June 8, 2026 (91 FR 34597).  No final rule had been published when this site was last checked.
